Cities of Refuge
SIT-eez uv REF-yooj
noun phrase (biblical institution)
From Hebrew 'ir miqlat ("city of refuge/asylum"); miqlat from qalat, "to take in, receive, gather." Six Levitical cities appointed in the Law (Num 35; Deut 19; Josh 20) as places of asylum for the manslayer.

See also: Cities of Refuge

Biblical Definition

The cities of refuge were six Levitical cities appointed under the Mosaic Law as places of asylum for a person who had killed another unintentionally, where he could flee from the avenger of blood and receive a fair trial. The Law established them at Num 35:9-34, Deut 19:1-13, and Josh 20: three cities on each side of the Jordan — Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron on the west; Bezer, Ramoth-Gilead, and Golan on the east. They were Levitical cities, evenly distributed so that no Israelite was far from refuge, with roads kept clear to them. The institution made a crucial moral distinction the surrounding cultures often blurred: between murder (intentional killing, which demanded the death penalty and from which the city gave no protection) and manslaughter (unintentional killing, for which the slayer could find asylum). The manslayer who reached the city was given a trial; if found to have killed without premeditation, he was protected from the avenger of blood, but he had to remain within the city until the death of the high priest, after which he could return home freely. The cities of refuge thus upheld both the sanctity of human life (the avenger's claim was real; blood was not cheap) and the justice of distinguishing intent (the unintentional slayer was not a murderer). The typology is rich and explicit in the Reformed tradition: the city of refuge prefigures Christ, the sinner's refuge from the just demand of the law and the wrath of God; the slayer's safety only within the city pictures the believer's safety only in Christ; and the slayer's release at the death of the high priest pictures the believer's full liberty secured by the death of our great High Priest (Heb 6:18, "who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us").

CITIES OF REFUGE, noun phrase. Hebrew 'ir miqlat; six Levitical cities of asylum under the Mosaic Law.

Established at Num 35:9-34, Deut 19:1-13, Josh 20: Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron (west); Bezer, Ramoth-Gilead, Golan (east).

Asylum for the unintentional manslayer fleeing the avenger of blood; with a fair trial distinguishing murder from manslaughter.

The slayer remained in the city until the death of the high priest, then returned home free.

A type of Christ, the sinner's refuge from the wrath of God (Heb 6:18); release at the high priest's death pictures liberty secured by our High Priest's death.

Key Scripture

Numbers 35:11-12 — "Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares. And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment."

Joshua 20:9 — "These were the cities appointed for all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them, that whosoever killeth any person at unawares might flee thither, and not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, until he stood before the congregation."

Hebrews 6:18 — "That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us."

Numbers 35:28 — "Because he should have remained in the city of his refuge until the death of the high priest: but after the death of the high priest the slayer shall return into the land of his possession."

Modern Corruption

The cities of refuge are corrupted when read as primitive blood-feud accommodation rather than a humane advance in justice, when the murder-manslaughter distinction is collapsed, or when the rich Christ-typology is missed in favor of mere historical curiosity.

expand to see more

Primitive-accommodation misreading. Modern readers sometimes view the cities of refuge as a quaint accommodation to a barbaric blood-feud culture — the law making the best of a violent age. The institution was in fact a profound advance in justice: it interposed a trial between accusation and execution, distinguished intent (murder vs manslaughter), protected the innocent slayer from private vengeance, and upheld the sanctity of life against both cheap killing and cheap acquittal. Far from accommodating barbarism, the cities of refuge tempered vengeance with due process — a principle modern justice systems rest on.

Typology-missed misreading. The cities of refuge are not merely an interesting Mosaic civil arrangement; the New Testament and the Reformed tradition read them typologically as a picture of Christ. The sinner, pursued by the just demand of the law (the avenger of blood), flees to Christ the refuge and is safe; he is safe only WITHIN the refuge (only in Christ); and the slayer's release at the death of the high priest prefigures the believer's full liberty secured by the death of our great High Priest. Heb 6:18 makes the connection explicit: we have "fled for refuge." To read the cities of refuge as bare history, missing the Christ they prefigure, is to read the shadow and miss the substance.
